titre: Diagnostic Performance of Radiomics-Based Machine Learning in Differentiating Glioblastoma From Brain Metastasis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Hong C, Liu G, Bie Z, Guo Y, Du Y, Hu Y, Li S, Liu P.
types: meta-analysis im systematic review review journal article
resume: Glioblastoma (GBM) and brain metastasis (BM) are the most common malignant intracranial tumors in adults. Noninvasive differentiation between them remains challenging, as they frequently share similar imaging features. Although radiomics-based machine learning (ML) models show promise, systematic evidence of their performance remains limited. We aimed to systematically estimate the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models in differentiating GBM from BM and to explore multiclass classification involving primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), thereby assessing their potential for clinical use. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 22, 2026, for studies reporting the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models for differentiating GBM from BM. Multiclass studies involving PCNSL were also retained. Methodological quality was appraised via the Radiomics Quality Score 2.0. Binary diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, stratified by internal and independent external validation. Multiclass sensitivities and specificities were pooled using separate joint generalized linear mixed models. Physician assessments were evaluated as an exploratory benchmark. A total of 39 studies (31 binary and 8 multiclass), involving 11,558 patients, were included. For binary classification, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.9% (95% CI 84.1%-92.4%) and 83.0% (95% CI 76.8%-87.9%) in internal validation, and 83.8% (95% CI 77.4%-88.7%) and 80.7% (95% CI 71.1%-87.7%) in external validation, respectively. In multiclass analyses, pooled sensitivity was 84.4% (95% CI 72.4%-91.8%) for GBM, 70.6% (95% CI 54.4%-82.8%) for BM, and 75.0% (95% CI 62.7%-84.3%) for PCNSL, with corresponding specificities of 82.5% (95% CI 70.1%-90.4%), 88.8% (95% CI 81.9%-93.3%), and 94.4% (95% CI 88.4%-97.4%), respectively. Radiomics-based ML models could distinguish between GBM and BM in the included cohorts. However, due to methodological limitations and scarce evidence, their generalizability and clinical utility remain unclear. Further multicenter prospective studies should conduct independent external validation in consecutive patients. PROSPERO CRD420261295269; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261295269.

titre: AI Predictive Models for Discharge Disposition in Patients Following Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Xie D, Chen R, Yue C, Liu X, Cao G, Jiao R.
types: meta-analysis systematic review review-article review journal article
resume: Background Although a growing number of AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in patients following primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA) have been constructed, their performance, quality, and applicability remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the performance, quality, and applicability of published AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in patients following primary TKA. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Database, China Science and Technology Journal Database, and SinoMed Database were searched from inception to May 26, 2025. We included original studies that developed AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in adult patients (age ≥18 years) undergoing primary TKA. Studies involving simultaneous bilateral or revision TKA or those that did not develop a predictive model were excluded. Risk of bias and reporting quality were assessed using the PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool+AI) and TRIPOD+AI (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis+AI), respectively. Pooled area under the curve values and 95% CIs were estimated using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochran Q test and I ² statistic. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to algorithm type, categorized as machine learning (ML)-based and deep learning (DL)-based models. Results A total of 5 retrospective studies from the United States involving 4 ML-based models and 1 DL-based model were included, with sample sizes ranging from 175,042 to 434,550 patients. Age and sex were the most frequently used predictors. All included studies were rated as having a high risk of bias according to the PROBAST+AI checklist. The pooled area under the curve was 0.75 (95% CI 0.67-0.82; I ²=99.9%; P I ²=99.8%; P P >.05). Conclusions AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition following primary TKA demonstrate a certain level of discriminative performance. However, the current evidence is limited, as all included studies were at high risk of bias and showed a high degree of heterogeneity. In addition, all included studies were conducted in the United States, which may limit the generalizability of these findings to other health care settings. Future studies should follow PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI checklists while developing and validating models across different countries and health care systems.

titre: External validation of an artificial intelligence-based ECG algorithm for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction: a prospective diagnostic cohort study.
auteurs: Champetier A, Lee MS, Lopez-Ayala P, Jo YY, Boeddinghaus J, Koechlin L, Bima P, Crisanti L, Zimmermann T, Kim K, Kim KS, Yoon S, Kaplan E, Gualandro DM, Recuenco LH, Huré G, Tsao TY, Nani M, Lee HS, K
resume: Background A novel artificial intelligence-based electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) model (AiTiA MI v2.00.00) for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was developed using data from Korean patients. Its performance in a European population remains unknown. Methods Patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected AMI were enrolled in two prospective European cohorts (APACE & APACE-Light; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00470587). The primary outcome was AMI, centrally adjudicated according to the fourth Universal Definition of MI. The AI-ECG model was applied to 12-lead ECGs recorded at ED presentation. Its diagnostic performance for AMI was directly compared to that of the BASEL score, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT), the recalibrated HEART score (all at ED presentation), and integrated physician judgment at 90 min, with the last two only available in APACE. Predefined AI-ECG triage thresholds for early rule-out and rule-in of AMI were also evaluated. Findings Among 12,630 patients with an available digital 12-lead ECG (5047 in APACE and 7583 in APACE-Light), adjudicated AMI was diagnosed in 19% (968/5047) and 18% (1386/7583) of patients, respectively. In patients with hs-cTnT at presentation (n = 5031 and n = 7565), the AI-ECG model showed good diagnostic performance for AMI with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.77-0.80) and 0.84 (0.83-0.85) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.56 (0.53-0.59) and 0.65 (0.62-0.67). Its discrimination was inferior to hs-cTnT (AUC 0.94 [0.93-0.95] and 0.93 [0.92-0.94]). The AI-ECG model provided some incremental diagnostic value when combined with hs-cTnT (AUC 0.95 [0.94-0.96] and 0.95 [0.94-0.95], p Interpretation AI-ECG showed high, but not very high, diagnostic accuracy for AMI. As a diagnosis of AMI is unlikely to be ruled out on ECG alone, combining AI-ECG with hs-cTnT may improve decision making in the ED, warranting prospective studies. Funding The Swiss National Science Foundation, the Swiss Heart Foundation, Innosuisse, the University Hospital Basel, the University of Basel, Abbott, Beckman Coulter, Idorsia, LSI Medience Corporation, Roche, Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Quidel, Siemens, SpinChip, Upstream, and Singulex, the Korea Health Industry Development Institute (KHIDI), funded by the Ministry of Health & Welfare, Republic of Korea (grant number: RS-2026-25543703).

titre: Behavior Change Techniques Associated With Abstinence in a Chat-Based Smoking Cessation Intervention: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial Using Machine Learning.
auteurs: Li Y, Su X, Cheung YTD, Zhao S, Lam TH, Wang MP, Luk TT.
types: research-article randomized controlled trial pragmatic clinical trial journal article
resume: Background Isolating the candidate intervention components that drive the success of digital behavioral interventions is crucial for understanding intervention mechanisms and optimizing future interventions. Objective This study aimed to identify behavior change techniques (BCTs) delivered in a chat-based smoking cessation intervention and determine their independent associations with biochemically validated abstinence. Methods This study is a secondary analysis of a pragmatic, cluster-randomized clinical trial conducted in Hong Kong. From June 18 to September 30, 2017, 624 adult daily smokers were recruited from 34 community sites and randomized to the intervention group. Participants received 3 months of personalized, real-time chat-based cessation support delivered by a live counselor via a mobile instant messaging app. The analytic sample included 230 participants (n=170, 73.9% male; mean age 43.0, SD 13.6 years) who engaged with the chat support. All chat dialogues during the real-time support were retrieved and systematically coded using an established BCT taxonomy for smoking cessation (BCTTsm). Four machine learning methods, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, Extreme Gradient Boosting, the Boruta algorithm, and recursive feature elimination, were used to identify the BCTs that are most predictive of biochemically validated tobacco abstinence outcomes at 3 and 6 months. A prespecified supermajority rule retained only BCTs selected by at least 3 of the 4 models for subsequent analysis. The stability of the selected BCTs was assessed using 500 bootstrap resamples for each model. Poisson regression with robust variance was subsequently used to examine the independent associations between the selected BCTs and abstinence outcomes. Covariates included sex, age, educational level, nicotine dependence, intention to quit in 30 days, and quit attempts at baseline. Results Systematic coding identified 35 distinct BCTs from the BCTTsm as having been delivered. Three BCTs were consistently selected by machine learning as the most predictive of both 3- and 6-month abstinence, with moderate to high stability (ranging from 61% to 100%): "provide rewards contingent on successfully stopping smoking" (BM4), "provide information on withdrawal symptoms" (RC6), and "provide information on consequences of smoking and smoking cessation" (BM1). In multivariable analyses, 6-month abstinence was significantly associated with BM4 (risk ratio [RR] 7.9, 95% CI 4.2-14.6), RC6 (RR 3.3, 95% CI 1.6-6.5), and BM1 (RR 2.7, 95% CI 1.4-5.5), with consistent results for 3-month abstinence. Conclusions Three BCTs, contingent rewards (BM4), information on withdrawal symptoms (RC6), and information on consequences (BM1), were identified as candidate intervention components associated with success in a chat-based smoking cessation intervention. This study is the first to apply machine learning for BCT identification, moving beyond simple frequency counts to data-driven feature selection. These findings provide empirical evidence for the candidate components of effective digital behavioral intervention that may warrant further testing and offer guidance for future intervention optimization.

titre: Image-Based AI for the Diagnosis of Retinopathy of Prematurity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Bai H, Zhou Y, Bai Y, Wang Y, Yang Y.
types: meta-analysis im systematic review review journal article
resume: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is one of the major causes of preventable blindness in premature infants. Early screening, accurate diagnosis, and severity classification are crucial for reducing irreversible visual impairment. Recently, image-based AI models have been widely applied to ROP screening, diagnosis, and severity classification. However, the model architecture, data source, validation method, and diagnostic task vary across studies. Consequently, the overall diagnostic efficiency and clinical utility of deep learning (DL) remain to be systematically assessed. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of image-based AI for ROP by disease type, validation method, model type, and use of transfer learning (TL). We performed a systematic search across Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, and Cochrane Library as of October 12, 2026, to identify studies investigating image-based AI for ROP detection or clinical subtype classification. The risk of bias (RoB) of included studies was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using bivariate mixed-effects models, with analyses stratified by diagnostic task and validation method. Sixty-two studies contributed 185 contingency tables. For normal vs ROP, pooled sensitivity was 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96) and specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97). For normal vs treatment-requiring ROP (TR-ROP), sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.91-0.99) and specificity was 0.74 (95% CI 0.66-0.80). For mild vs severe ROP, specificity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59-0.90). In external validation, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-0.97) and 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), respectively, while the corresponding estimates were 0.95 (95% CI 0.93-0.96) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) in internal validation. For DL and conventional machine learning (ML) models, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98), respectively, while specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97) and 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.94), respectively. With and without TL, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.97), respectively, while specificity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.86-0.95), respectively. Image-based AI may have high sensitivity for ROP assessment, but its specificity is lower for identifying TR-ROP and in the external-validation subgroup. Given the predominance of retrospective studies, heterogeneity, and limited external validation, current evidence supports AI as an adjunct to screening and referral, with clinicians retaining responsibility for diagnostic and treatment decisions. Prospective, multicenter external validation is needed. PROSPERO CRD420261418502; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261418502.

titre: Medical Interview Performance Using an AI-Based Standardized Patient vs a Human Standardized Patient: Randomized Crossover Trial.
auteurs: Yanagita Y, Yokokawa D, Fukuzawa F, Ihara S, Yoshida R, Sato R, Uehara T.
resume: Background In Japan, standardized patients (SPs) have traditionally been recruited to teach medical interview competencies. Recent advances in large language models have enabled increasingly natural conversational interactions, raising the possibility of using AI-based SPs (AI-SPs) for medical interview training. However, medical interview performance during interactions with AI-SPs compared with human SPs remains insufficiently understood. Objective This randomized single-center crossover trial aimed to compare medical interview performance and learner-reported experiences between encounters with a large language model-based AI-SP and a human SP. Methods Participants were fifth-year medical students undertaking clinical clerkships at Chiba University Hospital. The AI-SP was a text-based simulated patient implemented using GPT-4o. Participants were randomized to AI-SP followed by human SP, or the reverse. A washout period of at least 3 days was set between conditions. Each participant completed 2 cases, depression and appendicitis, in both conditions. For the AI-SP interviews, chat logs were retained, and a physician provided feedback after completion of the 2 cases. Human SP interviews were video recorded, and the physician portraying the SP provided feedback immediately after each interview. Medical interview performance was assessed using selected items from the Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX), with ratings performed independently by 2 general medicine specialists. Participants completed a self-rated questionnaire (7-point Likert-type scale) regarding learning satisfaction, perceived rapport formation, and active engagement in history taking. Results Forty-eight participants were analyzed. The Mini-CEX-based mean total score was significantly higher for the human SP than for the AI-SP (23.9, SD 1.7 vs 22.7, SD 1.7, respectively; mean difference 1.24; t 47 =3.7; P=.001). Scores for history taking and overall clinical competence were higher in the human SP condition. Interrater reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient of 2,1) was 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.83). No significant differences were found between conditions for learning satisfaction (human SP: mean 5.9, SD 1.1; AI-SP: mean 6.0, SD 0.8) or perceived rapport formation (human SP: mean 5.4, SD 1.3; AI-SP: mean 5.3, SD 1.3). Active engagement in history taking was significantly higher in the AI-SP condition (human SP: mean 5.8, SD 1.1; AI-SP: mean 6.2, SD 0.7; t 47 =2.7; P=.009). Conclusions Medical interview performance differed between the 2 SP conditions, with higher history taking and overall clinical competence scores in the human SP condition. The text-based nature of the AI-SP and the absence of nonverbal cues may have contributed to these differences. Although no significant differences between conditions were observed in most other assessment outcomes, learning satisfaction, or perceived rapport, self-rated active engagement in history taking was higher with the AI-SP condition. AI-SPs may offer a complementary modality for medical interview practice; however, this study assessed performance during simulated encounters rather than subsequent learning gains or performance with real patients. Trial registration UMIN Clinical Trials Registry UMIN000056228; https://center6.umin.ac.jp/cgi-open-bin/ctr_e/ctr_view.cgi?recptno=R000064153.
